qual_reasons:
  expression:
    clarity: Publication-ready prose; concrete, well-chosen words; no banned-register
      hits or padding; reads as polished SQLite documentation.
    coherence: Ideas progress smoothly; the fopen() framing recurs cleanly; each section
      has one job and transitions bridge naturally.
    concision: Every section earns its place; no replacement-history narration; tight
      throughout with cross-references rather than duplication.
  form:
    consistency: Mostly consistent, but spaced em-dash style appears (F2 rule 7),
      e.g. 'into one clause' constructs; minor casing drift in headings (Title Case
      vs sentence).
    formatting: Markdown renders cleanly; valid frontmatter, lists, links; footer-style
      'last updated' line present; no source artifacts.
    organization: Logical heading hierarchy, bulleted use-case list, numbered decision
      checklist arranged for the task; cross-references name what they point to; links
      target stable anchors.
  grounding:
    factuality: Claims largely corroborable against SQLite docs; the 2015 traffic
      stats are dated and self-reported but flagged 'as of this writing (2015)'; 281
      TB limit matches official spec.
    relevance: Every source and section bears on the when-to-use-SQLite purpose; the
      HN-discussion 'See also' is marked as supplementary; no performative citations.
    verifiability: Many claims linked to primary SQLite technical notes, but key quantitative
      claims (400-500K req/day, 15-20% dynamic, load average <0.1, ~200 statements)
      rest on a self-report dated 2015 without independent pointer.
  judgment:
    calibration: Mostly calibrated ('conservative estimate, not a hard upper bound'),
      but '100K hits/day' and 'almost always a better solution' assert thresholds
      without base-rate anchoring or ranges.
    fairness: Dedicated §2 and checklist argue the case against SQLite (concurrency,
      scale, network) at proportional depth; asymmetry openly declared (SQLite favored
      for device-local).
    robustness: Key claims mostly survive alternative lenses, but the 'competes with
      fopen()' framing is asserted as the obvious reading without testing the alternative
      that SQLite does compete with light client/server use.
  purpose:
    breadth: Covers the relevant use-case classes (embedded, app file format, websites,
      analysis, cache, server-side, transfer, archive, ad hoc, internal, testing,
      education) and the counter-cases.
    depth: Mostly well-developed, but several sections (experimental extensions, internal
      databases, education) are thin relative to their billing; SQLite write-concurrency
      'just works' claims under-quantified.
    scope: Scope declared up front (SQLite vs client/server, local app storage); body
      matches throughout with three clear sections of use cases, counter-cases, and
      a checklist.
    suitability: Task is named in the title and lede (when SQLite is appropriate vs
      client/server); answer recoverable from skim; output shape (guidance + checklist)
      fits the task.
  reasoning:
    discipline: Reasoning mostly moves cleanly observation->implication, but a few
      sentences blend observation and recommendation (e.g. concurrency advice) without
      naming the intermediate judgment.
    parsimony: Arguments are mostly minimal; the checklist re-derives points already
      made in §1-§2 (e.g. big-data/concurrency repeated), a mild redundancy in load-bearing
      chains.
    precision: Mostly specific (281 TB, 2^48, 100K hits/day, version numbers), but
      vague placeholders remain ('many applications', 'many people', 'systems designers
      report').
    soundness: Generally sound with named mechanisms (network latency, file locking),
      but some claims ('SQLite is often faster') asserted via developer reports without
      surfacing the assumption explicitly.

   points already made in §1-§2, a non-load-bearing repetition.

   `"SQLite supports databases up to 281 terabytes in size, assuming you can find a disk drive and filesystem that will support 281-terabyte files."`
   3\. Checklist For Choosing The Right Database Engine.
9. **Verifiability** (rule 2) *[partial]* — Quantitative website-traffic claims are
   self-reported and dated 2015 with no independent or current source pointer.
   *Location:*
   `"it handles about 400K to 500K HTTP requests per day, about 15-20% of which are dynamic pages touching the database."`
   Websites.
10. **Verifiability** (rule 1) *[partial]* — Some material claims stated without
    checkable referent ('demonstrated to work with 10 times that amount'). *Location:*
    `"SQLite has been demonstrated to work with 10 times that amount of traffic."`
    Websites.
11. **Factuality** (rule 4) *[partial]* — Traffic figures are 2015-era and may not
    reflect current scope, though the doc flags the date.
    *Location:* `"as of this writing (2015)"` Websites.
12. **Calibration** (rule 1) *[partial]* — Threshold claims (100K hits/day, ‘almost
    always better’) asserted without base-rate anchoring or stated range.
    *Location:*
    `"any site that gets fewer than 100K hits/day should work fine with SQLite."`
    Websites.
13. **Robustness** (rule 2) *[partial]* — The ‘competes with fopen()’ framing asserted
    as obvious without testing the alternative interpretation.
    *Location:* `"SQLite competes with [fopen()](http://man.he.net/man3/fopen)."`
    (lede).
